bib.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting

read.skipped: Plot axis fragments in Figs 22-24 and Table 6 cell text were skimmed, not studied.

question: How much does LLM accuracy change under meaning-preserving changes to prompt format, and how can that spread be estimated cheaply?
hypothesis: Formatting choices that preserve meaning should not change performance much, but the authors expect (and find) otherwise; they argue single-format reporting is misleading.
contributions: Show open LLMs are very sensitive to prompt formatting in few-shot settings, not removed by model size, shots or instruction tuning
Propose FormatSpread, a grammar of plausible formats plus Thompson-sampling bandit to estimate the min/max performance without model weights
Analyses of atomic perturbations, non-monotonic format space and format identifiability from prompt embeddings

method.summary: A manual grammar defines semantically equivalent prompt formats (casing, separators, spaces, enumeration styles). For 53 Super-NaturalInstructions tasks the paper samples formats, scores LLaMA-2, Falcon and GPT-3.5 few-shot, and reports performance spread (max minus min). FormatSpread uses Thompson sampling over formats under an evaluation budget.
method.task: few-shot classification and multiple choice; prompt-format sensitivity

datasets.name: Super-NaturalInstructions subset
datasets.size: 53 tasks (19 multiple-choice, 34 classification); datasets assumed size 1,000
datasets.split: few-shot examples random within each dataset and not used for evaluation; fixed order of evaluation samples
datasets.preprocessing: Tasks filtered: at least 1000 samples, instructions at most 3,000 characters, inputs at most 2,000 characters, at most 20 distinct outputs, not 0% on LLaMA-2-7B 1-shot, at most 4 tasks per source dataset; formats added to socially impactful tasks lacking one

datasets.name: SuperNaturalInstructions open-ended generation subset
datasets.preprocessing: Instructions under 1,000 chars, inputs under 5,000 chars; generation limited to 50 tokens and cut at first newline

inference.decoding: not stated for classification; scoring by exact prefix match of output or ranking of options by model probability
inference.samples: 10 random formats per task for Sec 4.2; 500 formats x 250 samples for Sec 4.3 on 31 tasks; 320 formats with E=40,000 evaluations for LLaMA-2-70B and GPT-3.5; 1- and 5-shot; one fixed set and order of few-shot examples per task
inference.prompting: inst c p(D1) c ... c p(Dn) c p(Dn+1), spacing '\n\n' between instruction and examples; n-shot with n in {1,5}

parameters.Thompson prior: Beta(alpha,beta), beta=5, alpha=max(beta*x/(1-x),1.1), x = original format accuracy
parameters.search: E/2 budget for best format then E/2 for worst, second prior reuses counters

other.format_embedding: last hidden layer of prompt, 4,096-dim for LLaMA-2-7B; XGBoost on top-n PCA components, 800 vectors per format train, 200 test, 10 formats

metrics.name: ranking accuracy
metrics.definition: rate that the expected answer is the highest-ranked valid option by the model's output distribution

metrics.name: exact prefix matching accuracy
metrics.definition: output prefix matches expected answer after normalization of casing, spacing, newlines

metrics.name: performance spread
metrics.definition: max_i m(p_i,D) - min_i m(p_i,D) across plausible formats

metrics.name: centered mass
metrics.definition: ratio of examples where output matched any valid option regardless of correctness

eval.protocol: McNemar one-sided tests (p<0.05) on 1000 samples for model-comparison reversals; 5 trials averaged over 31 tasks for Fig 9; 100 trials for Fig 8; ranking accuracy by default

availability.data: Super-NaturalInstructions (public); 53 task ids listed in App B.1

prompts.purpose: illustrative 1-shot prompt (not from a real task)
prompts.text:

results.claim: Equivalent formats move accuracy by up to 76 points on LLaMA-2-13B and about 10 on average.
results.quote: with accuracy varying in up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats, and ∼10 accuracy points on average across 50+ tasks and several models.

results.claim: Median spread across 10 random formats per task.
results.setup: 53 tasks, 10 sampled formats, LLaMA-2 and Falcon, 1- and 5-shot, ranking accuracy; lower bound
results.quote: a median spread of 7.5 accuracy points across choices in the model and the number of few-shot examples

results.claim: Probability that a lead of at least 2 points for LLaMA-2-13B over -70B reverses under another format.
results.quote: LLaMA-2-13B and -70B reverse trend by at least d = 0.02 with probability 0.141

results.claim: Same reversal for LLaMA-2-7B vs Falcon-7B.
results.quote: LLaMA-2-7B and Falcon-7B reverse trend by at least d = 0.02 with probability 0.140

results.claim: Share of reversal cases where both experiments were significant (13B/70B pair).
results.setup: one-sided McNemar, p<0.05, 1000 samples; second value 47% for the 7B/Falcon pair
results.quote: 76% and 47% respectively for the two model comparisons
results.note: 76% here is not the 76 points above

results.claim: Pairwise format ordering preserved across models only slightly above chance.
results.table: Table 3, row Llama-2-7b / Llama-2-13b, column Performance Relative Ordering Preservation
results.note: Text says < 0.62 probability; Table 3 prints 'Falcon-2-7b' for Falcon-7b

results.claim: LLaMA-2-70B 1-shot median spread over 320 formats.
results.quote: yields a median spread of 0.171 (mean=0.221, std=0.200, using probability ranking across 53 tasks; 25% of tasks had a spread of 0.292 or higher, with a maximum spread of 0.876)

results.claim: LLaMA-2-70B 1-shot maximum spread.
GPT-3.5 median spread over 320 formats, with a spread up to 56 points, under 10 USD per task.
results.quote: we find a spread up to 56 accuracy points with a median spread of 6.4 accuracy points with GPT3.5 across 320 formats and 53 tasks at a cost of under 10USD on average per task.

results.claim: With 51,200 evaluations Thompson sampling is within 1 point of true spread; naive within 4; UCB within 11.
results.quote: With a budget of 51,200 evaluations, Thompson sampling results in a spread within 1 accuracy point of the true spread, while naive sampling finds a spread within 4 points, and UCB within 11.

results.claim: 5% of the search space suffices to estimate spread within 2 points.
results.setup: task with 2,500 test examples and 320 formats
results.quote: we are able to estimate spread within 2 accuracy points of the true spread

results.claim: About 17% of tasks gain at least 5 points of spread going from 10 to 20 formats.
results.quote: about 17% of tasks are expected to increase their spread by at least 5 accuracy points when increasing from 10 to 20 sampled formats

results.claim: Atomic changes with at least 5 points accuracy change (exact prefix matching).
results.quote: 24% of atomic changes have an associated accuracy change of at least 5 points when using exact prefix matching as scoring criteria (11% when using probability ranking)

results.claim: Monotonic triples are no more frequent than chance, so local search is ineffective.
results.setup: 24 tasks, 300 triples each, 250 samples, exact prefix matching
results.quote: 32.4 and 33.6% of triples were monotonic for multiple-choice and non-multiple-choice tasks respectively

results.claim: Separators S1 strongly differ in 22% of tasks; Fitem2 in 10%.
results.table: Table 1, row S1, column Strong Diff.

results.claim: Top 100 principal components identify the format with at least 0.98 accuracy.
results.setup: LLaMA-2-7B prompt embeddings, 10 formats, 31 tasks, XGBoost
results.quote: using just the top 100 principal components can result in a classifier with ≥0.98 accuracy in format identification for all 31 tasks analyzed

results.claim: Format-identifiability correlates moderately with spread.
results.quote: (0.424, p = 8.04 · 10−6; 0.555 for the 5-shot setting; using exact prefix matching)

results.claim: Exact prefix matching accuracy tracks centered mass for falcon-7b-instruct 1-shot.
Exact prefix matching gives larger median spread than ranking.
results.quote: with median spread ranging from 12 to 28 accuracy points depending on the model used

results.claim: Single-constant edit raises task280 accuracy from 0.043 to 0.826.
results.setup: probability ranking, model not named in Table 2

results.claim: Prompt length does not explain spread (ranking).
Authors say a single well-working format is acceptable for building systems.
results.quote: choosing a single prompt format that works sufficiently well for use in this larger system is a valid methodological choice

limits: Equivalent formats are semantically equivalent by the grammar but some are unusual for humans (e.g. <sep>, ::); parsing choices create odd strings in under 20% of cases (App C)
Only short instructions and inputs; effect of input length left to future work
Only descriptor casing, separators, spaces, enumeration vary; wording, instructions and examples fixed
Spread from 10 formats is a lower bound and grows with more formats; no noise floor or confidence interval on spread
GPT-3.5 uses prefix matching, LLaMA ranking, so medians not comparable; LLaMA-2-70B 4-bit quantized
Models are LLaMA-2, Falcon-7B, GPT-3.5-Turbo (dated); few-shot only
The 31-task analyses use a task set not fully named; Fig 20 lists task ids outside the 53
